newsitem.title: UK: Hambros managers quit after Co-op probe.
newsitem.headline: Hambros managers quit after Co-op probe.

text.p: Britain's Hambros on Thursday parted ways with three of its key bankers and promised to tighten controls after a probe said its role in the failed bid for the Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) fell short of good business practice.
Andrew Regan, the man behind the bid, was quick to say he thought the advice given to his Galileo bidding vehicle had been lacking and he was wrong to rely on his City advisers.
"The events of this week make it perfectly clear that the advice Galileo paid so many millions of pounds for, and followed every inch of the way, was inept," Regan said in statement.

On Tuesday Nigel Campion-Smith, the lawyer who acted for Regan, resigned as a partner at law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite because he felt responsible for the embarrassment the CWS affair had caused.

While law firm Norton Rose found those involved in the bid at Hambros had not had any dishonest intent, its independent inquiry said their conduct "fell well short of the standards of good business practice".

City watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) said it would study the report, which has also been passed to the Bank of England, and decide whether it need to undertake its own probe or take action against Hambros or the individuals concerned.

Hambros advised entrepreneur Andrew Regan's Galileo and Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica in a discredited 1.2 billion pound ($2 billion) bid for mutually-owned supermarkets-to-funeral parlours group CWS.

"I always believed I could rely on my City advisers, but the unpublished report obviously shows that I was wrong to do so," Regan said. In April Hambros made an unreserved apology to the Co-op over its conduct and paid a substantial sum, reported to be around a million pounds, to the group.

Regan's bid collapsed after a sustained counter-attack through the courts by CWS and the withdrawal of key financial backing for the ambitious plan. Hambros backed the bid to the bitter end, despite repeated questioning by CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth about the use of confidential CWS documents.
Regan, his business associate David Lyons and former CWS manager Allan Green, face possible prosecution by Britain's Crown Prosecution Service which took over a private CWS action against them.
CWS accused Regan and Lyons of "aiding, abetting, counselling or procuring the theft and for handling stolen property". Green is accused of theft of confidential documents.

Bankers said the latest development was another blow to Hambros' attempts to build up its corporate finance activities. Last month its deputy chairman Michael Sorkin said its support for Regan would have an impact on business but the impact would be modest.
"This is probably the end of Hambros as a major force in corporate finance," one corporate financier said. "They have been struggling for some time."

The resignation of Nigel Pantling -- head of the corporate finance division and the highest level casualty of the affair -- would be particularly damaging to the firm in what is an essentially relationship-driven business, bankers said.
Hambros said he would be replaced by 42-year-old William Nabarro, an executive director of the bank. Nabarro has been head of Hambros corporate finance office in Leeds, north-west England.

Two corporate financiers directly involved in the bid, Peter Large and Andrew Salmon, have also resigned with immediate effect although they will be paid three months' salary in accordance with their contracts.
Hambros also said a number of members of staff were subject to internal disciplinary measures.
Corporate financiers said Pantling, a well-respected and "impressive" figure in the City, was likely to find a job elsewhere.
Banking sources said Hambros was not likely to make any further comment on the episode, satisfied it had carried out a full inquiry into the events.
"Its in the hands of the regulators," said one.

The report found those at Hambros who knew that confidential information from CWS had or might become available without proper authority "failed to appreciate that it was not appropriate for them either to receive or use that information".
As a result of the recommendations of the investigation, Hambros said it would introduce changes to tighten internal controls and bring in some additional procedures.

These include client and transaction clearance procedures, a strengthening of the compliance function and its relationship with the corporate finance division and "a number of other improvements and safeguards in systems".

Hambros said it was not possible to publish the report for legal reasons but it will introduce the changes suggested as quickly as possible, in full consultation with its supervisors, and will institute further reviews of high level internal controls. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
